title: Replace a Faucet
summary: Swap a kitchen or bathroom faucet for a new one, and if you want, replace the old shutoff valves under the sink with reliable quarter-turn ones.
safety: Shut off the water and open the faucet to prove it's off before disconnecting anything. When replacing the valves, the main water must be off. Use two wrenches so you never twist the pipe in the wall. Wear glasses when working under the sink.
pro: the pipe behind the valve is too short, corroded or cracked, you have old galvanized pipe, a valve needs soldering, or the main won't shut off completely. Replacing a faucet usually doesn't need a permit; changing pipes may. Check with your local building department.

questions.label: How many holes in the sink or counter?
Bathroom: spread of the outer holes
questions.hint: Center to center. Skip for a kitchen.

questions.label: How does the pipe connect to the shutoff valve?
Valve top to faucet connection
questions.hint: Measure straight up from the valve outlet to the underside of the sink at the faucet hole.

calcNote: Lines come in 12", 16", 20", 24" and 30". This adds about 2" so the line can curve without kinking.

steps.t: Check your sink and pick the faucet
steps.idea: The new faucet must fit the holes in your sink.
steps.b:
1. Look under the old faucet (or under the sink) and count the holes in the sink or countertop.
  2. Bathroom with 3 holes: measure center to center of the outer holes. About 4" = centerset, 8" or more = widespread.
  3. Kitchen: count all holes, including the sprayer, soap pump or a dishwasher air gap.
  4. Buy a faucet made for that layout. A single-hole faucet can cover 3 holes with its deck plate.
  5. Read the faucet's instructions now: they say what supply line size you need and whether to use putty.
faq: Can I fill an unused hole?
Yes, with a sink hole cover, or use it for a soap pump.
What's that thing in the 4th hole?
If it's a small dome connected to the dishwasher, it's an air gap. Some areas require it. Leave it in place.

steps.t: Clear and look under the sink
steps.idea: Room to work and a photo of how it all connects.
steps.b:
1. Empty the cabinet. Lay a towel on the cabinet floor.
  2. Take a photo of the connections.
  3. Find the two shutoff valves (angle stops): hot on the left, cold on the right.
  4. Look at how the pipe enters each valve. A nut on the pipe = compression. Threads into the valve = threaded. Soldered joint = sweat. A collar with no nut = push-fit. Update the answer at the top.
  5. Measure from the top of each valve to the faucet hole. Enter it above to get the supply line length.

steps.idea: {{a.newvalves==='yes'?'You\'re replacing the valves, so the whole house must be off.':'Close the two valves under the sink.'}}
steps.b:
1. {{a.newvalves==='yes'?'Turn off the main water valve. Turn the handle clockwise, or a lever crosswise to the pipe.':'Turn each angle stop clockwise until it stops. Quarter-turn valves: 90 degrees.'}}
  2. Open the faucet, hot and cold. Water should stop within a few seconds.
  3. {{a.newvalves==='yes'?'Open a faucet on the lowest floor (or an outdoor spigot) to drain the pipes.':'If it keeps running, a valve is not closing. Shut off the main and plan to replace that valve.'}}
  4. Leave the faucet open.
steps.stop: Old valves can break if forced. If a handle won't turn, or it leaks around the stem when you turn it, stop and shut off the main instead.
faq: Where's the main?
Usually where the water line enters: basement, crawlspace, garage, or by the water heater. Some are at the meter in a box by the street (needs a meter key).

steps.idea: Undo both lines at the valve, holding the valve still.
steps.b:
1. Put the bucket under the valves.
  2. Hold the valve body with one wrench.
  3. With the second wrench, turn the line's nut counterclockwise (as you look down the line toward the valve).
  4. Let the water in the line drain into the bucket.
  5. If the old lines are rigid tubes, you'll replace them: just loosen both ends.

steps.idea: Pull-down and side sprayers connect under the sink.
steps.b:
1. Find where the sprayer hose joins the faucet below the sink.
  2. Quick-connect: squeeze the clip or press the collar and pull the hose off.
  3. Threaded: unscrew it with pliers.
  4. Unclip the weight from the hose and pull the hose up through the faucet.

steps.idea: Free the old drain linkage so the faucet can lift out.
steps.b:
1. Find the flat metal strap (clevis) hanging behind the drain.
  2. Squeeze the spring clip and slide the horizontal pivot rod out of the strap.
  3. Loosen the screw on the strap and pull the lift rod up from above.
  4. Keeping the old drain? Leave the rest alone.

steps.idea: Big nuts on the faucet's shanks hold it to the sink, high up behind the bowl.
steps.b:
1. Lie on your back in the cabinet with glasses on. Grit falls.
  2. Find the mounting nuts on the faucet shanks, up against the underside of the sink.
  3. Set the basin wrench jaw on a nut so it tightens as you turn counterclockwise (seen from above).
  4. Turn the T-bar. Repeat on each nut.
  5. Plastic wing nuts usually unscrew by hand.
faq: The nut won't move.
Spray penetrating oil, wait 15 minutes. Corroded plastic nuts can be cut off carefully with an oscillating tool. Don't cut into the sink.

steps.t: Lift out the faucet and clean the deck
steps.idea: A clean, flat surface lets the new gasket seal.
steps.b:
1. Lift the faucet straight up. Wiggle it if putty holds it.
  2. Scrape old putty and mineral rings off with a plastic scraper.
  3. Wipe with vinegar, then water, and dry.
  4. Check the sink around the holes for cracks.
faq: Can I use a metal scraper?
Not on porcelain, stainless or stone: it scratches. Plastic only.

steps.idea: Unscrew the valve, then pull the old nut and ferrule off the pipe.
steps.b:
1. Make sure the main is off and the lines are drained.
  2. Hold the valve body with one wrench. Loosen the nut where the pipe enters (counterclockwise) with the other.
  3. Pull the valve straight off the pipe. The old nut and brass ferrule stay on the pipe.
  4. Thread the old nut onto the sleeve puller and turn the handle until nut and ferrule come off.
  5. Check the pipe: round, smooth, not gouged, and at least about 3/4" sticking out from the wall plate.
  6. Clean the end with a rag or fine emery cloth.
steps.stop: If the pipe is cracked, kinked, or too short after removing the ferrule, don't force a fitting on. It needs a repair (often soldering): call a plumber.

steps.idea: New nut, new ferrule, pipe pushed in all the way, then tighten.
steps.b:
1. Slide the wall plate (escutcheon) on if it was removed.
  2. Slide the new nut onto the pipe, threads facing out toward the valve.
  3. Slide the new ferrule on. If one end is longer or tapered, point that end toward the valve.
  4. Push the valve onto the pipe until it bottoms out. Turn it so the outlet points up.
  5. Thread the nut on by hand.
  6. Hold the valve with one wrench and turn the nut about 1/2 turn past hand-tight with the other.
  7. Close the valve (turn the handle off) before you turn the main back on.
faq: Can I reuse the old ferrule?
No. Once squeezed, a ferrule has taken the shape of the old joint. Use the new one that comes with the valve.
Should I tape the threads?
No tape on compression threads. The ferrule makes the seal.

steps.idea: Unscrew the old valve from the iron pipe nipple and screw on a new one with sealed threads.
steps.b:
1. Hold the pipe nipple sticking out of the wall with the pipe wrench.
  2. Turn the old valve counterclockwise with the adjustable wrench to unscrew it.
  3. Clean the threads with a rag or wire brush.
  4. Wrap PTFE tape 3-4 times clockwise around the threads (looking at the pipe end), or brush on thread sealant.
  5. Screw the new valve on by hand, then 1-2 turns with the wrench while holding the nipple, stopping with the outlet pointing up.
  6. Close the valve before turning the main back on.
steps.stop: If the nipple turns in the wall, is rusted thin, or breaks, stop. Old galvanized pipe can snap inside the wall: call a plumber.

steps.idea: Cut the pipe just behind the old valve, then install a push-fit stop on the clean pipe.
steps.b:
1. Check there is enough straight, clean pipe behind the valve: at least the push-fit's insertion depth plus about 1/2".
  2. Clamp the tubing cutter on the pipe just behind the valve. Tighten the knob a little and spin it around. Repeat until it cuts through.
  3. Deburr the inside and outside of the cut end.
  4. Mark the insertion depth with the gauge or marker.
  5. Push the new stop on straight until the mark meets the fitting. Tug it: it should not come off.
  6. Turn the outlet up and close the valve before turning the main on.
steps.stop: If the pipe is too short to cut and still fit a new valve, it needs soldering or a new pipe stub. That's a job for a plumber, or for someone experienced with a torch.
faq: Can I use a compression valve instead?
Yes, on round, clean copper with enough length. Push-fit is quicker and forgiving for beginners.

steps.idea: Release the old valve with a clip, check the pipe, push on the new one.
steps.b:
1. Snap the disconnect clip around the pipe against the fitting's collar.
  2. Push the clip into the collar and pull the valve off at the same time.
  3. Inspect the pipe end: if it's scratched or bent, cut off 1/2" with the tubing cutter and deburr.
  4. Mark the new insertion depth.
  5. Push the new valve on until the mark meets the fitting. Tug it.
  6. Close the valve before turning the main on.
faq: My pipe is PEX.
Push-fit stops work on PEX. Check the fitting has a PEX insert (stiffener), as most do.

steps.t: Turn the main back on and check the valves
steps.idea: Pressure test the new valves before the faucet goes in.
steps.b:
1. Check both new valves are closed.
  2. Close any faucet you opened to drain the house, leaving one upstairs faucet open to let air out.
  3. Turn the main on slowly.
  4. Watch the new valves for 5 minutes. Wipe them dry and touch with a tissue.
  5. A weeping compression nut: tighten 1/8 turn more while backing up the valve.

steps.t: Seat the faucet on the sink
steps.idea: The gasket (or putty, if the maker says) seals the faucet base to the sink so water can't get under it.
steps.b:
1. Unbox and lay out the parts. Compare them to the instruction diagram.
  2. Put the rubber gasket or deck plate under the faucet base as shown.
  3. Use plumber's putty only if the instructions call for it. On marble, granite or other stone, use stain-free putty or silicone.
  4. {{a.room==='kitchen'?'Feed the supply lines and hose down through the hole.':'Feed the shanks (or lines) down through the holes.'}}
  5. Have a helper hold the faucet straight from above.
faq: Gasket or putty?
Most new faucets use a gasket and no putty. Putty under a gasket can make it leak.

steps.idea: Snug the mounting nuts so the faucet doesn't twist, without cracking anything.
steps.b:
1. Thread the washer and mounting nut onto each shank by hand. Many new faucets use a long nut you tighten with a screwdriver or the included tool.
  2. Check from above that the faucet is straight and centered.
  3. Tighten with the basin wrench or tool until the faucet can't turn.
  4. Stop at firm. Overtightening cracks porcelain and plastic nuts.

steps.t: Connect the pull-down hose and weight
steps.idea: The weight retracts the spray head; it must hang free.
steps.b:
1. Feed the spray hose down through the faucet.
  2. Push the hose onto the quick-connect until it clicks. Tug to check.
  3. Clip the weight on the hose at the point marked in the instructions.
  4. Pull the spray head out and let go: it should glide back and dock.
  5. Move anything in the cabinet that the loop could catch on.
faq: Head won't retract all the way.
Move the weight lower on the hose, and make sure the hose isn't rubbing on the supply lines or the trap.

steps.idea: Optional: a new drain matches the faucet and fixes old leaks.
steps.b:
1. Loosen the slip nut on the trap and remove the old drain's big nut from below. Push the old drain body up and out.
  2. Clean the hole.
  3. Put the new drain's seal under its flange: the gasket, or a rope of putty if the maker says.
  4. From below, add the rubber gasket, washer and big nut. Line the pivot hole toward the back.
  5. Tighten the nut by hand, then a little more with pliers until snug.
  6. Put in the stopper, slide the pivot rod through it, and hand-tighten the pivot nut.
  7. Connect the lift rod to the strap and set the height so the stopper opens about 1/2".
  8. Reconnect the trap.
faq: Overflow hole?
If your sink has an overflow hole, the drain body's side holes must line up with it. Use a drain with overflow.

steps.idea: Braided lines from the valves to the faucet, hot to the left.
steps.b:
1. Check the faucet end of each line matches the faucet (1/2" or 3/8" thread, or a 3/8" compression end).
  2. Thread the faucet end on by hand, then 1/4 turn with a wrench.
  3. Hot (left) to the left valve, cold (right) to the right.
  4. Thread the 3/8" compression nut onto the valve outlet by hand.
  5. Hold the valve with one wrench and turn the nut 1/4 to 1/2 turn past hand-tight.
  6. Lines should curve gently: no kinks.
faq: Lines too long?
A loop is fine. Never cut a braided line.

steps.t: Flush the lines and the aerator
steps.idea: Clear grit from the work before it clogs the new faucet.
steps.b:
1. Unscrew the aerator from the spout tip (or pull-down head) counterclockwise. Use the key that came with the faucet, or tape on the pliers' jaws.
  2. Slowly open the shutoff valves fully.
  3. Run hot and cold for about a minute each.
  4. Rinse the aerator screen and screw it back on.
faq: Water sputters at first.
That's air in the pipes. It clears in a minute.

steps.idea: Every joint you touched gets a dry-tissue test now and again tomorrow.
steps.b:
1. Run the faucet for a minute, hot then cold.
  2. Run a dry tissue around each valve, each supply nut, the faucet shanks{{a.room==='bath'?', and the drain nut':', and the hose connection'}}.
  3. Fill the sink and let it drain to test the drain.
  4. Leave a dry paper towel on the cabinet floor overnight.
  5. Check again tomorrow. A spot on the towel shows any slow drip.
faq: Drip at a compression nut.
Tighten 1/8 turn more, backing up the valve. Still dripping: shut off, take it apart, and check the line is seated straight.
Hot and cold are reversed.
Swap the lines at the valves.

basinWrench.b:
1. Flip the jaw so it faces the direction you want to turn.
  2. Reach up and hook the jaw on the nut. The spring holds it in place.
  3. Turn the T-bar. The jaw bites harder as you turn.
  4. To loosen as seen from above, turn counterclockwise. From below, that feels like clockwise.
  5. If the jaw slips, flip it over and try again.

twoWrench.b:
1. Put one wrench on the valve body (or fitting) you don't want to move.
  2. Put the second wrench on the nut you're turning.
  3. Push the two handles toward each other, or hold one still and turn the other.
  4. Nothing behind the valve should move.

compressionHelp.b:
1. Pipe end clean, round and cut square.
  2. Nut on first, threads facing the fitting. Then the ferrule.
  3. Push the pipe into the fitting until it stops.
  4. Hand-tight, then about 1/2 turn with a wrench while backing up the fitting.
  5. Test. If it weeps, 1/8 turn more. No tape.

leakCheck.b:
1. Wipe every joint dry.
  2. Run the water.
  3. Touch each joint with a dry tissue. Any wet mark is a leak.
  4. Check again after an hour and the next day.

basin.title: Use a basin wrench
basin.cap: The spring-loaded jaw grabs the nut up behind the bowl where no other wrench fits. Turn the T-bar; the jaw tightens on the nut as you turn.

compression.svg: <text x="10" y="16" class="k">Compression fitting, cut in half</text><rect x="160" y="70" width="90" height="60" rx="3" class="tb"/><text x="214" y="104" text-anchor="middle">valve</text><rect x="10" y="88" width="172" height="24" class="y"/><text x="30" y="104">pipe</text><rect x="110" y="70" width="54" height="14" class="bk"/><rect x="110" y="116" width="54" height="14" class="bk"/><path d="M124 88 L142 84 L160 88 Z" class="af"/><path d="M124 112 L142 116 L160 112 Z" class="af"/><text x="60" y="52" class="k">nut</text><line x1="76" y1="54" x2="116" y2="70" class="o"/><text x="150" y="52" class="ac">ferrule (sleeve)</text><line x1="160" y1="56" x2="142" y2="82" class="a"/><text x="10" y="152">1  Slide on the nut, threads toward the valve.</text><text x="10" y="164">2  Slide on the ferrule.</text><text x="10" y="176">3  Push the pipe in all the way, then tighten.</text>
compression.cap: Tightening the nut squeezes the brass ferrule onto the pipe: that ring makes the seal, not the threads. No tape needed.

puller.svg: <text x="10" y="16" class="k">Pull off an old ferrule</text><rect x="10" y="40" width="10" height="100" class="b"/><rect x="20" y="86" width="140" height="20" class="y"/><rect x="110" y="74" width="34" height="44" rx="2" class="bk"/><rect x="144" y="74" width="60" height="44" rx="3" class="tl"/><rect x="160" y="92" width="110" height="8" class="inkf"/><rect x="266" y="70" width="8" height="52" rx="3" class="w"/><text x="64" y="60" class="k">old nut + ferrule</text><line x1="110" y1="62" x2="126" y2="74" class="o"/><text x="204" y="60" class="k">puller body</text><line x1="112" y1="134" x2="162" y2="134" class="a" style="stroke-width:2"/><polygon points="162.0,134.0 156.6,136.6 156.6,131.4" class="af"/><text x="170" y="137">nut and ferrule come off</text><text x="10" y="162">Turn the handle: the screw pushes on the pipe end.</text>
puller.cap: Thread the old nut onto the puller, then turn the handle. Don't pry or twist the ferrule off with pliers: you'll gouge the pipe and the new valve won't seal.

pushfit.svg: <text x="10" y="16" class="k">Push-fit: square cut, mark the depth</text><rect x="20" y="86" width="180" height="20" class="y"/><line x1="150" y1="78" x2="150" y2="114" class="a" style="stroke-width:2"/><rect x="212" y="74" width="80" height="44" rx="4" class="bk"/><rect x="212" y="74" width="10" height="44" rx="2" class="tl"/><text x="256" y="100" text-anchor="middle">push-fit stop</text><line x1="200" y1="132" x2="212" y2="132" class="a"/><polygon points="212.0,132.0 206.6,134.6 206.6,129.4" class="af"/><text x="20" y="70">cut square, deburr</text><text x="132" y="134" class="ac" text-anchor="end">depth mark</text><text x="230" y="66">release collar</text><text x="10" y="160">Push in until the mark touches the fitting.</text>
pushfit.cap: Use the depth gauge from the maker (often about 1" for 1/2" pipe). If the mark isn't at the fitting's face, the pipe isn't in far enough to seal.

supplyconn.svg: <text x="10" y="16" class="k">Connect the supply lines</text><rect x="10" y="30" width="300" height="8" class="tl"/><rect x="214" y="38" width="10" height="36" class="bk"/><rect x="208" y="66" width="22" height="14" rx="2" class="y"/><rect x="72" y="140" width="16" height="16" rx="2" class="bk"/><rect x="73" y="128" width="14" height="12" rx="2" class="y"/><rect x="88" y="144" width="14" height="8" rx="2" class="y"/><circle cx="80" cy="166" r="8" class="bk"/><path d="M80 128 C80 60 219 140 219 80" class="o" fill="none" style="stroke-width:4"/><text x="236" y="60" class="k">faucet end:</text><text x="236" y="72">hand-tight</text><text x="236" y="84">+ 1/4 turn</text><text x="110" y="138" class="k">valve end, 3/8" comp:</text><text x="110" y="150">hand-tight + 1/2 turn</text><text x="10" y="190">Hold the valve with a second wrench.</text>
supplyconn.cap: Braided lines with a rubber cone seal at the faucet end need no tape. Gentle curves only: a kink restricts the flow and can burst.

weight.svg: <text x="10" y="16" class="k">Hose and weight</text><rect x="10" y="60" width="300" height="8" class="tl"/><rect x="150" y="24" width="14" height="36" rx="3" class="bk"/><path d="M157 24 Q157 8 196 12 L204 26" class="o" fill="none" style="stroke-width:4"/><rect x="152" y="68" width="10" height="30" class="bk"/><path d="M157 98 V150 Q157 182 187 182 Q217 182 217 150 V104 H226" class="o" fill="none" style="stroke-width:3"/><rect x="178" y="174" width="20" height="14" rx="2" class="inkf"/><rect x="222" y="98" width="10" height="12" rx="2" class="y"/><text x="222" y="152" class="k">weight</text><text x="222" y="164">at the low point</text><text x="238" y="98" class="k">quick-connect</text><text x="238" y="110">click, then tug</text><text x="10" y="120">hose hangs free:</text><text x="10" y="132">nothing in the</text><text x="10" y="144">way of the loop</text>
weight.cap: The weight pulls the spray head back into the spout. Place it where the maker's instructions say, usually at the bottom of the loop with the head docked.

popup.svg: <text x="10" y="16" class="k">Bathroom pop-up drain</text><rect x="30" y="40" width="100" height="12" class="tb"/><rect x="170" y="40" width="120" height="12" class="tb"/><rect x="120" y="34" width="60" height="6" class="bk"/><rect x="136" y="40" width="28" height="110" class="bk"/><rect x="126" y="52" width="48" height="6" class="mp"/><rect x="122" y="58" width="56" height="10" rx="2" class="y"/><rect x="164" y="90" width="14" height="12" rx="2" class="y"/><line x1="150" y1="96" x2="252" y2="112" class="o" style="stroke-width:3"/><rect x="250" y="58" width="8" height="80" class="bk"/><line x1="254" y1="20" x2="254" y2="58" class="o" style="stroke-width:2"/><circle cx="252" cy="111" r="4" class="af"/><text x="10" y="30">putty or gasket</text><line x1="92" y1="30" x2="124" y2="36" class="o"/><text x="10" y="66">gasket + big nut</text><line x1="96" y1="64" x2="120" y2="62" class="o"/><text x="176" y="150" class="k">pivot rod</text><line x1="200" y1="142" x2="200" y2="108" class="o"/><text x="266" y="30">lift rod</text><text x="266" y="80">clevis</text><text x="266" y="92">strap</text><text x="10" y="182">Use putty only where the maker says.</text>
popup.cap: The lift rod behind the faucet moves the clevis strap, which tilts the pivot rod and lifts the stopper. Hand-tighten the pivot nut: it only seals the rod.

aerator.svg: <text x="10" y="16" class="k">Flush out the debris</text><rect x="20" y="44" width="140" height="18" rx="6" class="bk"/><rect x="140" y="44" width="22" height="40" rx="4" class="bk"/><rect x="140" y="100" width="22" height="12" rx="2" class="y"/><line x1="144" y1="106" x2="158" y2="106" class="th-l"/><line x1="151" y1="88" x2="151" y2="98" class="a"/><polygon points="151.0,98.0 148.4,92.6 153.6,92.6" class="af"/><circle cx="132" cy="124" r="2" class="inkf"/><circle cx="140" cy="128" r="2" class="inkf"/><circle cx="168" cy="124" r="2" class="inkf"/><rect x="190" y="44" width="90" height="18" rx="6" class="bk"/><rect x="258" y="44" width="22" height="40" rx="4" class="bk"/><rect x="262" y="84" width="14" height="40" class="wt"/><line x1="220" y1="126" x2="310" y2="126" class="o"/><text x="10" y="146" class="k">1  Unscrew the aerator</text><text x="10" y="158">(tape on the jaws if</text><text x="10" y="170">you need pliers)</text><text x="184" y="146" class="k">2  Run hot + cold</text><text x="184" y="158">for 1 minute, then</text><text x="184" y="170">rinse and refit it</text>
aerator.cap: New valves and disturbed pipes shed grit. Flushing without the aerator keeps it from clogging the new faucet or its cartridge.

glossary: The shutoff valve under the sink. Its outlet points up at 90 degrees to the pipe.
A joint sealed by a brass ring (ferrule) squeezed onto the pipe by a nut.
The brass ring in a compression fitting. Also called a sleeve or olive.
A fitting that grips a pipe when you push it in. Brand names include SharkBite.
Female iron pipe: inside pipe threads.
Bathroom faucet hole spreads: 4" and 8" or more, center to center.
The screen in the spout tip that mixes air into the stream.
A long-handled wrench with a swiveling jaw for nuts behind a sink.
The round cover plate where the pipe comes out of the wall.
